chief_complaint: tender red swollen lump with foul discharge on back
hpi_details: A 74-year-old woman has a previously intermittent back lump that became tender, red, swollen, and foul-smelling over several days, concerning for an infected epidermoid cyst or abscess.
ideas: She thinks an old harmless fatty lump on her back was bitten by a spider or scratched in the shower and turned into a painful boil.
concerns: She is worried that the rapid swelling and foul odor mean the lump has turned into a flesh-eating infection or skin cancer.
expectations: She hopes the doctor will numb the area, drain the foul fluid, and prescribe antibiotics so she can sleep on her back again.

clinical_knowledge.topic: Infected Sebaceous Cyst evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Infected Sebaceous Cyst is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Standard management emphasizes incision and drainage when a fluctuant abscess is present; antibiotics are reserved for systemic illness, extensive cellulitis, immunocompromise, or other high-risk features and should reflect local pathogen risk.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: tender red swollen lump with foul discharge on back
Key HPI features: A previously intermittent back lump became tender, red, swollen, and foul-smelling over several days.
Objective/Exam findings: Focused physical exam and vital signs check. Tailored diagnostics for Infected Sebaceous Cyst.
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Infected Sebaceous Cyst.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Soft tissue infection without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Missing systemic infection or features concerning for a necrotizing soft-tissue infection.
management_principles: Incision and drainage when a fluctuant abscess is present; selective antibiotics for systemic illness, extensive cellulitis, immunocompromise, or other high-risk features
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

teaching.one_liner: Plastic and reconstructive surgical case presenting with tender red swollen lump with foul discharge on back.
differentials: Soft tissue abscess unrelated to a cyst
red_flags: Fever, hypotension, confusion, rapidly spreading cellulitis, or severe systemic illness requiring urgent emergency evaluation
Pain out of proportion, skin discoloration or bullae, crepitus, or rapidly progressive swelling suggesting a necrotizing soft-tissue infection

must_ask.say: How long has this lump been there, and when did it become red and painful?
Have you had this lump before, or noticed it getting bigger and smaller over time?
What does the discharge look like, and does it have a bad smell?
Have you had any fever or chills?
Do you have diabetes or anything that affects your immune system?

history.answer: I have had a bump on my back for years, but over the last four days it got red, swollen, and started leaking foul-smelling pus.
I first noticed a tiny painless lump on my back about five years ago, but it suddenly swelled up and became painful four days ago.
It is right in the center of my upper back, between my shoulder blades.
It was the size of a small marble for years without changing, but over the past four days it swelled up to the size of a golf ball.
There is only this single lump on my back, and I have not found any bumps anywhere else on my body.
It used to feel firm and movable under my skin, but now it feels very tight, swollen, and somewhat squishy.
It aches constantly with a throbbing pain, and it hurts sharply whenever anything touches it or presses against my back.
No, I haven't noticed any moles changing color, shape, or size, and this lump has always been skin-colored.
It hasn't had recurring crusts, ulcers, or active bleeding; it just started leaking cloudy fluid yesterday.
Yes, the skin over and around the bump is bright red, warm to the touch, and the drainage smells quite foul.
There is a tiny dark pore in the center, and when it started draining, thick yellowish-white cheesy material came out.
In the past it would occasionally puff up a tiny bit and then calm down, but it never blew up like this before.
No, I have never had severe back acne, a cut, surgery, or any piercing in that area.
No, I have not had any fever, chills, night sweats, or unexplained weight loss.
I rarely expose my back to direct sunlight, and I have never had a severe blistering sunburn.
No, neither I nor anyone in my family has ever had skin cancer or melanoma.
I don't have diabetes, I have never received an organ transplant, and I don't take any immunosuppressant medications.
I tried gently pressing on it two days ago when it swelled up, but it hurt too much, so I just put a clean bandage over it.
I've had this quiet little lump for years, but I think a bug bit it and turned it into an angry boil.
With that terrible smell and the red swelling, I'm scared to death it might be skin cancer or a flesh-eating bug.
I'm hoping you can numb it and drain the fluid today, then give me antibiotics so I can finally sleep on my back.
I don't have any chronic illnesses like high blood pressure, diabetes, or heart disease.
I have never had any surgeries or hospital admissions in my life.
I am not taking any prescription medicines, over-the-counter painkillers, or herbal supplements.
I do not have any known allergies to medicines, foods, or latex.
I have never smoked cigarettes or used any tobacco products.
I only drink half a glass of wine on rare social occasions once or twice a year.
I am a retired elementary school teacher, and I live with my husband in an apartment.
My parents passed away in their eighties from natural old age, and there is no family history of skin diseases.

exam.finding: Alert, comfortable-appearing elderly female in no acute respiratory or toxic distress.
Blood pressure 124/78 mmHg, pulse 74 bpm, respiratory rate 16 breaths/min, temperature 36.8°C, and oxygen saturation 99% on room air.

Upper back shows a 3 cm tender, erythematous, fluctuant subcutaneous nodule with a central punctum and malodorous purulent drainage, non-transilluminating and mobile over underlying tissue, with no other lesions elsewhere.
No palpable enlargement or tenderness of occipital, posterior cervical, or supraclavicular lymph nodes.
No palpable axillary lymphadenopathy on either side; breast tissue without focal masses.
Clear breath sounds bilaterally without wheezes, rales, or rhonchi.
Regular rate and rhythm with normal heart sounds; no murmurs, rubs, or gallops heard.
No spinal bony tenderness over the thoracic vertebrae; intact thoracic spine mobility.
